blocks.title: Honors — spiral the toolkit
blocks.markdown: Today's CPA practice mixes the kinematics moves you've built — position, velocity, acceleration, the equations of motion. The honors demand isn't to get more answers. It's to **say why your chosen equation was the right one**, and to make every hidden assumption stand in the open.

blocks.title: Name the assumption
blocks.markdown:
Almost every kinematics equation you reach for carries a silent claim: **constant acceleration over the interval.** $v = v_0 + at$ and $\Delta x = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2$ are only true if $a$ doesn't change while the clock runs.

Before you plug in, ask: *is $a$ actually constant here, or am I assuming it?* On a problem where it isn't (a car that brakes, then coasts, then accelerates), one equation across the whole trip is a lie. You'd have to break the motion into intervals where the assumption holds.

## Solve, then name what you assumed

Work the CPA problem set as written. But for **each** problem, before you trust the number, write one line in the margin: *the assumption I made to use this equation is ___.* Constant acceleration? A clean start from rest? Motion in a straight line so I can treat position as a single signed number? Most kinematics errors aren't arithmetic — they're an assumption that didn't actually hold.

blocks.frame: I chose the equation ___ for this problem. It was the right choice because the givens were ___ and the unknown was ___. The assumption it rests on is ___, and I know that assumption holds here because ___.
blocks.prompt: JUSTIFY (homework): Pick the hardest problem from today's set. Don't just show the work — defend the *choice* of equation. Why that one and not another? What assumption does it carry, and how do you know that assumption is safe for this particular problem?

blocks.frame: If I had to predict 2026-XJ's position from its current velocity, the kinematics assumption I'd be leaning on is ___. It could fail because ___.
blocks.prompt: TRANSFER (homework): Soon you'll predict where 2026-XJ is at graduation from its velocity today. Which kinematics assumption would that prediction rest on — and name one reason it might quietly break over a year-long flight.
